html:
Wootz is a high carbon steel made in sealed clay pots in south India and Sri Lanka, and Golconda in the Deccan was one of its best known sources in the 1600s.

Smiths heated iron with plant matter in small closed crucibles until it melted and soaked up carbon. The result was a cake of steel that, when forged, gave a blade both hard and tough, with a wavy pattern on its surface. The method was very old.

The cakes were traded to Persia and Syria, where smiths turned them into the famous Damascus sword blades. In the age of the Qutb Shahi sultans of Golconda, Indian steel was still prized across the Islamic world.

European scientists were fascinated. In the early 1800s Michael Faraday and others ran tests on wootz, and a Russian engineer managed to copy the pattern. By then the Indian craft was dying out, undercut by cheap imported steel. It sits beside the Iron Pillar of Delhi as a sign of how skilled Indian metalwork was.
sum: Wootz is a high carbon steel made in sealed clay pots in south India and Sri Lanka, and Golconda in the Deccan was one of its best known sources in the 1600s.
